BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A brief dry but continued gusty period is likely late Saturday into early Sunday as the first system moves east and another deep low approaches the coast.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry Wednesday through early Friday. Near record high temperatures.
- Chance of precipitation returns Friday night, with additional rain and mountain snow, along with cooler temperatures, through the weekend into next week.
- Breezy winds this week, increasing and becoming windy Friday through Sunday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Skies are partially clearing early this morning as a weak system moves east across the Idaho Panhandle. This will allow patchy fog to develop this morning. Otherwise, a weak warm front will lift north across the area today, producing clouds but no precipitation across the north. To the south, it will be mostly sunny today with highs several degrees warmer than Monday. Winds will be lighter today. An upper level ridge will amplify to our east across the interior western US Wednesday and Thursday while an upper level trough deepens in the eastern Pacific. This will bring mild temperatures, dry conditions, and breezy south to southeast winds. Highs will be 15-20 degrees above normal and near record highs each day, with lower valleys reaching the mid 60s to around 70F. Skies will be mostly clear with a few high clouds passing overhead.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A deep trough will approach the coast on Friday, increasing southwest flow across the area. It will become windy across the open terrain of southeast Oregon and far southwest Idaho with gusts 35-50 mph, and 20-40 mph elsewhere. Highs on Friday will remain near record highs, warmest across southwest Idaho. The trough will weaken as it moves inland, but will push a cold front across the area late Friday into Saturday with rain and high mountain snow. Precipitation chances will rise to 50-80% Friday night through Saturday morning, highest across the mountains. Rainfall amounts will be light in the valleys with light to moderate totals in the mountains. Snow levels will fall from 7-8kft MSL Friday evening to 6-7kft by Saturday morning, keeping snowfall confined to higher mountains. Winds will remain gusty on Saturday, but not as strong as Friday. Highs Saturday will cool 5-10 degrees.

A brief dry but continued gusty period is likely late Saturday into early Sunday as the first system moves east and another deep low approaches the coast. This next system will gradually move inland Sunday and Monday, bringing a 40-60% chance of precipitation to the area throughout the two day period. Chances will likely increase/decrease across narrower periods as confidence in timing and details rises in subsequent forecasts. Winds will slacken but continue to be breezy as the trough moves in and the surface pressure gradient weakens. Temperatures will remain similar on Sunday, then cool several more degrees on Monday as colder air arrives with the trough. Snow levels should also decrease to 4-6kft by Monday. Precipitation chances trend lower on Tuesday, but troughing overhead will keep conditions unsettled with temperatures cooling a few more degrees.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: For the advertised system over the weekend, models appeont wiar to be trending more bullish on the rain and snow potenital for both the mountains and the plains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will likely prevail through Friday.
- Increasing chances for light mountain rain/snow showers by this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Our trend of above normal temperatures (10-15 degrees), continues as today's high temperatures will be in the upper 60s and lower 70s for the plains. More cloud cover is expected as a shortwave tracks north of Colorado today and into the Great Plains Wednesday. This shortwave also allows the push of a weak front into our region this afternoon/evening increasing wind gusts up to 20-30 mph along the area of the Cheyenne Ridge. Elevated fire weather conditons will be possible, but relative humidity values are expected to stay above critical thresholds. The passage of this weak front will cause Wednesday's high temperatures to be slightly lower in the low to mid 60s.

Quiet weather will continue through the rest of the work week as the upper level ridge axis dominates our area through Friday. High temperatures will be in the mid to upper 60s, but a few solutions favor reaching or exceeding 70F. At this time, the chances of temperatures exceeding 70F are about 20-40% for Thursday and Friday.

For the advertised system over the weekend, models appeont wiar to be trending more bullish on the rain and snow potenital for both the mountains and the plains. Generally, a low pressure system moves into SW Colorado and Northern New Mexico Saturday evening before lee- cyclogenesis produces a potential surface low near far southeastern Colorado. This will give us our next chance for snow showers for the higher terrain and rain for the plains. Intensity and placement of this low/trough will likely determine accumulation totals. Cooler temperatures are also expected with highs on the weekend in the upper 50s and lower 60s. Monday should be a pleasant fall day before our next storm system moves in around mid-week.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday-Monday...West to southwest flow aloft prevails, and with minimal low and mid level moisture, chances for precipitation will be limited. Maximum temperatures will be similar each day, from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Windy conditions are expected today; however, critical fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.
- Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue into and through the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: It will be another pleasant, but windy day ahead of us here across the forecast area, more on the winds in a bit. First lets take a quick look at the synoptic set-up aloft, there will be a weak shortwave that will slide across the CWA from a weak system that passes just to our northeast. We will remain dry as all model guidance indicates other than a slight increase in high-level clouds. Speaking of winds, they will once again be the main story as we see 700 mb winds ramp up into the 35 to 45 knot range by later this morning. A surface low near the Black Hills will develop an push east through the morning hours, as it does so, it will pull the surface trough east with it away from the Laramie Range along with pulling the gusty winds east into the High Plains by this afternoon. With ample subsidence, expect gusts at the surface up to 50 mph, but there is the possibility of stronger gusts in the known wind prones. Our in-house guidance indicates a slim chance for high winds at are known wind prone areas along I-25 and I-80 at this time. Then, by this evening, expect the winds to begin to wind down. A by product of this wind event will be fire weather concerns, as dry as it has been coupled with these gusty winds, elevated fire weather concerns are expected for this afternoon. Then switching gears to temperatures, with the strong westerly downsloping winds, it will lead to a warm day across portions of the CWA, primarily east of the Laramie Range. So, expect highs west of the Laramie Range to top out in the mid 50s. While highs along and east of the I-25 corridor will soar into the mid to upper 60s, possibly a few 70s. Lows Tuesday night will bottom out generally in the mid to upper 30s, with a few valleys west of I-25 seeing lows tank to around 30. As we head into Wednesday, look for relatively quiet conditions to return as ridging builds back in, bringing back in a northwest flow regime. Look for continued dry and breezy conditions along with slightly cooler temperatures, well, compared to Tuesday. So, highs Wednesday will generally top out in the mid 50s west of I-25 and low to mid 60s east of the corridor. Lows will bottom out Wednesday night in the lower 30s west of the Laramie Range and upper 30s to lower 40s to the east.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday...As a ridge aloft moves further eastward across Wyoming and 700 mb temperatures rise to near 6 Celsius, a warming trend will begin with high temperatures from the upper 50s to upper 60s.
Friday...Ridging aloft moves overhead centered from western North Dakota to eastern Colorado, with maximum temperatures similar to those of Thursday.

Saturday...A progressive negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft moves into western Wyoming, spreading increasing mid and high level cloudiness across our counties, with low POPS across southern Carbon County, for rain and snow showers, including the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Slightly cooler with the increase in cloud cover.

Sunday-Monday...West to southwest flow aloft prevails, and with minimal low and mid level moisture, chances for precipitation will be limited. Maximum temperatures will be similar each day, from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Models indicate the potential for several low pressure systems across the Western CONUS this weekend into next week. Each of these waves have the potential to bring cooler and wetter conditions to our area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures will continue through the work week.
- The pattern is looking more active this weekend into next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure will persist through the week, bringing warmer and drier conditions. Temperatures are expected to run 5-10 degrees above normal through at least Friday. A quick moving system to our north will bring increased cloud cover on Tuesday, as well as maybe some breezy winds across northeast Utah and northwest Colorado.

Models indicate the potential for several low pressure systems across the Western CONUS this weekend into next week. Each of these waves have the potential to bring cooler and wetter conditions to our area. The first arrives this weekend, and precipitation amounts are not terribly concerning. In general the snow levels appear to range from 7-9 kft, which is lower than previous storms. Beyond that model agreement remains poor this far out, so be sure to stay tuned to see how the forecast develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Dry weather should last into Tuesday, but by late in the day another long wave trough amplifies over the western United States, and this system shows the potential to bring beneficial snow to the mountains during the mid/late week period next week. \/Hodanish

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warm today with a weak, dry, cool front pushing across the region in the afternoon.
- A bit cooler tomorrow, then mild into late week.
- Showers possible over the region Saturday into early Sunday.
- Dry Monday, then another strong system by mid/ate week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today will be another nice mild day across the region. MAx temps will once again be in the 65-70F range with mid 50s in the valleys. A cool front will cross the region during the afternoon. The fropa will likely be rather subtle, with a windshift likely mostly being felt in the El Paso county region. The front will be dry.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Temps will be about 3 to 6F cooler on Wednesday than today. Temps will rebound for Thursday and Friday. Dry weather will continue.

For the weekend, the first in a series of weather systems will move across the region. This system will have the potential to bring some showers to all of the region, with the best chance of seeing some high elevation snows over Contdvd region. The shower activity should move out of the region by midday Sunday as ridging once again builds over the area.

Dry weather should last into Tuesday, but by late in the day another long wave trough amplifies over the western United States, and this system shows the potential to bring beneficial snow to the mountains during the mid/late week period next week. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Global deterministic models are in fairly good agreement bringing the next trough into the area for Saturday. This progressive system would bring a quick shot of widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild conditions will persist areawide through a majority of the week, with the next chance for precipitation arriving this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad ridge over the area today will give way to a weak shortwave trough that is currently rippling through the PacNW and western Nevada. Some high clouds will continue to cross Utah ahead of it, otherwise little moisture will be available as this trough crosses Utah Tuesday morning. Main impact will be some cold advection on Tuesday under a northwesterly flow. While temperatures in the valleys will cool slightly, stronger cooling aloft should weaken the inversions in place, clearing out some of the valley haze. After the trough exits the area, a strong ridge will return to the area Tuesday night through late week.

Global deterministic models are in fairly good agreement bringing the next trough into the area for Saturday. This progressive system would bring a quick shot of widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the area. However, cluster analysis of global ensembles show a 50/50 split between this wet solution and a drier solution where the trough remains well offshore.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. You may encounter wet, loose avalanches on steep south and southwest aspects in the afternoon, particularly near rock outcrops.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, holding too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow features if you find them below ridges or in deeper gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches. On isolated slopes at higher elevations, you might encounter stiffer slabs over weak layers 1 to 2 feet deep on the north side of the compass. Look for stiffer snow surfaces or rounded drifts below ridges or deeper gullies as features to avoid, especially in steep, consequential terrain.
